title: I split a ten year NQ backtest by hour, found the one hour holding the entire loss, filtered it out, and the result got $6,093 worse
author: person-person12
selftext:
This is a mistake I made last night and the numbers came out clean enough to be worth posting.

Setup: NQ, 5 minute candles, first 30 minutes of the session builds a range, first close outside it takes the break, one trade a day, both directions, stop 1 ATR, target 1 ATR, flat by 15:55. One contract from $50,000, May 2016 to August 2026. 2,562 trades, 49.9% wins, profit factor 0.96, finished at $26,259.

Then I grouped those same 2,562 trades by the hour the entry fired:

**14:00 UTC**, 1,269 trades, **+$14,159**, profit factor 1.05

**15:00 UTC**, 917 trades, **-$42,765**, profit factor 0.81

16:00 UTC, 225 trades, +$1,714, profit factor 1.04

everything later, 151 trades, +$3,150 between them

One bucket is more than the entire loss. So the fix looked obvious, only take the break inside the first hour after the range closes. I wrote that as a real rule, 60 minute window, changed nothing else, and ran the same ten years again.

**2,185 trades, 49.7% wins, profit factor 0.94, finished at $20,166.**

It removed 377 trades and came out **$6,093 worse** than leaving them in.

**\_\_\_\_\_**

The reason is daylight saving. Those buckets are UTC, and 14:00 UTC is 10am Eastern from March to November and 9am Eastern from November to March. A 9am Eastern entry cannot exist in this strategy because the range isnt finished until 10. So the summer 10am trades sat in the 14:00 bucket and the winter 10am trades sat in the 15:00 bucket, next to the summer 11am ones. The bucket I was going to delete was half the good trades wearing the wrong clock.

The genuinely late breaks, the 377 the window actually removed, made about +$6,100 between them.

**\_\_\_\_\_**

The thing doesnt work either way, and thats the bill rather than the clock. $25,620 of commission and slippage across 2,562 round turns at $2.50 a side and half a tick. Before costs the same trades made +3.76% over ten years, so the edge was worth roughly $1,900 gross and the execution came to thirteen times that.

I ran all of it in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading), which is mine, and grouping a result by hour is one click in there, which is exactly how easy it was to talk myself into cutting a fifth of the trades on a number that was not measuring what I read it as.

comments.author: SuperOrbital_Trading
comments.body: Lesson learned. Standardize all data sets to the same time zone.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Agreed, and its worth checking even when youre sure everything is already sitting in one zone. In this one the hour bucket was correct, and the filter took out trades that were paying for the rest of the sample.

replies.author: SuperOrbital_Trading
replies.body: It is amazing how you can spend hours creating, versioning, verifying, and back testing and still end up with a loser because of some tiny little mistake. What is worse is hunting down an issue, fixing it, then still losing. So I feel ya. But, you can't make an omelet without cracking some eggs as the saying goes.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Yea, and the worse version is when the fix is correct and the number still goes the wrong way, which is what happened here. Took me most of a day to accept that the hour I removed **wasnt the problem**.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
Good catch, and the DST bucketing trap goes beyond session-hour analysis. Anything anchored to an exchange or agency wall clock (the 9:30 ET open, 8:30 ET macro prints, 2:00 PM ET FOMC) moves in UTC twice a year, so any UTC-bucketed study quietly mixes two different regimes. The fix is to store event and bar times as timezone-aware timestamps in the source's local zone, bucket by that zone, and only convert to UTC for storage.

This matters even more for event-driven work. If you tag bars relative to a release time, a one-hour DST slip puts pre-release bars in the post-release window, and the backtest looks better for the wrong reason. It's the same discipline we've had to build into EventTrader at Cymetica: every event carries its canonical local release time plus a UTC equivalent, so windows stay aligned across DST.

Nice writeup on the sanity check, too. Deleting the "bad" bucket and seeing the result get worse is a cheap test everyone should run. [https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH](https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH)

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
Youre right, and the release version is the one that would have caught me out. My candle times are stored **timezone aware and bucketed in Eastern**, so the 9:30 open is still the 9:30 open through both flips, but I dont tag anything relative to a print yet.

How wide a window do you tag around a release before you call a candle post-event?

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
There isn't one cutoff that works everywhere, so I'd use a few tiers instead of a single line. The bar that contains the release timestamp is its own category. Don't count it as either pre or post, because a 1-minute bar opening at 8:29 and closing at 8:30 has the print inside it. A bar counts as pre-event only if it closes at or before the release, and as post-event only if it opens at or after.

After that, I'd split the post window into buckets like 0 to 1 minutes (spreads and slippage are worst here, and fills in a backtest are the least believable), 1 to 5, 5 to 30, and 30 to 60. Then check how the result changes as you widen or narrow them. If your effect only shows up in one bucket, that tells you something, and if it disappears when you shift a boundary by a minute, it was probably an artifact. For pre-event, a short blackout of a few bars before the print is common, since positioning and spread widening start early.

A couple of specifics: FOMC has two events, the 2:00 statement and the 2:30 press conference, so tag them separately. Also, an 8:30 print lands before the cash open, so for equities the "post" window mostly shows up in futures and pre-market until 9:30, which is worth keeping in mind when you compare.

Are you working on futures or cash equities?

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
Agreed on the containing candle, thats the one that always gets counted twice. A candle opening 8:29 and closing 8:30 has the print sitting inside it and it ends up in whichever bucket you happened to write first.

The 0 to 1 minute bucket is the one I trust least for exactly the reason you said, the fill is the least believable part of it. Do you cut the buckets on the clock, or on the first candle that moves more than some multiple of the prior range?

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
I cut on the clock, because a bucket defined by the first big candle is defined by the outcome. If the boundary depends on how far price moved, you've conditioned on the thing you're trying to measure, and the "post" window will always look more eventful than it really was. It also makes different prints incomparable, since the window starts at a different time each day.

What I'd do is keep the buckets on fixed clock times and record the range multiple as a separate descriptive tag, for example "first post-release bar moved more than 2x the prior 20-bar average range." That way you can split results by reaction size afterward without moving the boundaries. If you want the thresholds to adapt to volatility, scale them by pre-release ATR, computed before the print, so nothing in the definition looks at the outcome.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Youre right, and thats cleaner than what I did. **If the boundary moves with the size of the reaction then the post window is selected for being eventful**, which is the same mistake the post was about, one layer down. Fixed clock buckets with the range multiple recorded as a tag you can split on afterwards keeps the windows comparable across prints.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Exactly. One more thing that helps once you have the tag: when you split by reaction size, use fixed cut points you write down beforehand (like above and below 2x), or terciles computed only from prior prints, so the splits themselves aren't chosen after seeing which one looks good. And keep the sample per print type in mind, since CPI and FOMC give you only about a dozen observations a year, so a split into several buckets gets thin quickly. Good luck with it.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Writing the cut points down first is the part I have to force on myself. Choosing a split after seeing which one looks best is **the same overfit in a different hat.** The thin sample is the worse problem, since three buckets on a dozen CPI prints leaves four observations each. How many would you want per bucket before trusting it?

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
There's no magic number, but I'd want at least 20 to 30 per bucket before reading anything into a difference, and even then only for large effects. With four per bucket, one odd print can flip the result. At a dozen CPI prints a year, the practical answers are to pool across similar event types (CPI, PPI, NFP) after checking that they behave alike, to go back several years, or to use two buckets only. Pooling intraday windows from the same release doesn't add independent observations, since they all share one print.

Also, when the sample is that small, report the effect with a confidence interval instead of a bucket average, and treat anything that doesn't clearly separate from zero as "no evidence yet" rather than a finding. To force the habit of writing cut points first, commit them to a timestamped file or a git commit before you run the analysis.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Youre right, and the pooling point is the one I hadnt thought through properly. Four intraday windows off one CPI print is **one observation, not four.** At 20 to 30 per bucket a ten year window gets me two buckets and thats it, so Ill redo it with two and a confidence interval instead of the bucket average. Did CPI, PPI and NFP behave alike enough for you to pool them, or did you have to keep them apart?
